sidebar.ctaText: Book a consultation and review the safest next step.

body: Kidney stones are hard deposits that form in the kidney when minerals collect in urine. A stone may stay in the kidney or move into the ureter, which is the tube that carries urine to the bladder.
Small stones may pass with medicines and monitoring. Larger stones, blocked stones, infected stones, and repeated stones need proper urology care.

subsections.title: Symptoms
body: Common symptoms include sharp pain in the side, back, lower abdomen, or groin. You may also notice burning urine, blood in urine, nausea, vomiting, fever, or repeated urinary infections.
Some small stones cause no symptoms. They may be found during ultrasound, CT scan, or a routine health check.

subsections.title: When to consult a urologist
body: Consult a urologist if pain is severe, pain keeps coming back, urine is blocked, fever is present, blood appears in urine, or a scan shows a stone.
Urgent care is needed if stone pain comes with fever, chills, vomiting, weakness, or reduced urine.

subsections.title: Diagnosis and tests
body: Tests may include urine test, blood test, ultrasound, X-ray KUB, CT KUB, kidney function test, urine culture, and stone analysis when a stone is passed or removed.
The aim is to know stone size, stone location, kidney swelling, infection risk, and kidney function.

experience.title: Treatment options for kidney stones
body: Treatment depends on stone size, stone location, pain, infection risk, kidney swelling, and kidney function.

Common procedures include URS for ureter stones, RIRS for selected kidney stones, PCNL or mini PCNL for larger stones, ECNL for very large or complex stones, and laparoscopic surgery in special cases.

careGuide.title: Before, during, and after stone treatment
careGuide.intro: Good stone care includes safe treatment and a prevention plan.

tabs.label: Before Treatment
items: Share fever, vomiting, or severe pain history
Tell the doctor about medicines and allergies
Follow fasting instructions if surgery is planned

tabs.label: During Treatment
items: Confirm stone side and procedure name
Ask about URS, RIRS, PCNL, ECNL, or stent if relevant

tabs.label: After Treatment
items: Attend stent removal or follow-up scan

careGuide.note: Your plan will depend on stone size, location, infection risk, kidney function, and overall health.

items.question: Can a kidney stone pass without surgery?
items.answer: Some small stones can pass with medicines, fluids, and monitoring. Larger, stuck, infected, or painful stones may need a procedure.

items.question: What is URS?
items.answer: URS is ureteroscopy. A thin scope is passed through the urine passage to treat a stone in the ureter.

items.question: What is RIRS?
items.answer: RIRS is retrograde intrarenal surgery. A flexible scope is used to reach selected kidney stones and break them with laser.

items.question: What are PCNL and ECNL?
items.answer: PCNL treats larger kidney stones through a small back opening. ECNL may be used for very large or complex stones.

items.question: Is laparoscopic surgery common for stones?
items.answer: No. Most stones do not need laparoscopic surgery. It may be used in selected complex cases.

items.question: How can I prevent stones again?
items.answer: Prevention may include more fluids, diet changes, stone analysis, urine tests, and follow-up based on your stone type.
